abstract: Solid oxide fuel cells (SOFCs) are a new type of fuel cell that directly converts chemical energy into electrical energy and have received considerable attention in recent years [1,2]. High-temperature (800–1000 °C) SOFCs are efficient, pollution-free electrochemical converters with broad fuel adaptability (hydrocarbons, alcohols, and ammonia) [3]. However, at intermediate temperatures (500–700 °C), material degradation and a decrease in cathode performance compromise the efficiency of SOFCs [4,5]. Sluggish oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) kinetics at the cathode are widely recognized as key factors limiting the performance of SOFCs [6,7]. Therefore, many researchers are dedicated to developing novel cathode materials with superior electrochemical performance.

abstract: Ferroelectric (FE) materials, which exhibit switchable spontaneous polarization, have long provided the foundation for a broad range of electronic and energy storage applications [1−6]. In addition to conventional ferroelectrics, antiferroelectrics (AFEs) and relaxor ferroelectrics (RFEs) offer distinct polarization behaviors that arise from their antipolar or nanoscale-disordered dipole configurations [7−9]. More recently, materials exhibiting relaxor antiferroelectric (R-AFE) behavior, where long-range antipolar order is disrupted by compositional or structural disorder, have gained attention as promising candidates for advanced dielectric energy storage applications [10−12]. Within this category, R-AFEs are especially appealing because of their slim polarization-electric field (*P*–*E*)...

They provide an alternative to traditional chemical batteries and facilitate the self-powering of microelectronic devices, including biomedical implants, aerospace equipment, and Internet of Things (IoT) nodes [5,6]. A significant challenge to the widespread adoption of IoT technology lies in the self-powering power demands of critical components, such as sensors and wireless transceivers.

abstract: Flash sintering (FS) is a novel field-assisted sintering technique (FAST) in which ceramic materials are simultaneously subjected to a critical electric field and furnace temperature [1]. This method gives rise to a series of unique physical phenomena, including rapid densification, conductivity surge, and visible luminescence [1−4]. Since its first report in 2010, yttria-stabilized zirconia (YSZ) ceramics—particularly 3 mol% (3YSZ) and 8 mol% (8YSZ)—have been widely studied as models in flash sintering [1,5−7]. To date, flash sintering has been successfully expanded to multiple ceramic systems [8]. However, the underlying mechanism governing the onset of flash sintering is still not well understood, significantly limiting further advancements in this technique.

abstract: With the continuous development of aeroengine technology, ceramic matrix composites (CMCs), i.e., SiCf/SiC composites, have emerged as the most promising alternatives to replace traditional high-temperature alloys [1−3]. CMCs exhibit superior properties, including excellent high-temperature resistance, low density, and high strength, and their application in hot-end components can effectively improve the thrust-to-weight ratio of engines [4−6]. However, CMCs easily oxidize or suffer from severe recession when exposed to water‒oxygen environments during service [7,8]. Therefore, protective coatings need to be prepared on the surface to increase their durability under harsh engine operating conditions.

abstract: Recent advancements in optoelectronic technologies have driven the demand for multifunctional luminescent materials capable of operating across multiple spectral regions to increase device performance and application versatility [1−3]. In particular, materials exhibiting both visible (Vis) and near-infrared (NIR) emissions hold great promise for applications in optical communication, bioimaging, photocatalysis, and photovoltaics [4−6]. While Vis emission is crucial for lighting and displays [7−9], NIR light offers superior tissue penetration, making it highly suitable for biomedical imaging and diagnostics [10−12]. Therefore, dual-emission materials represent a compelling platform for integrated optoelectronic systems.

abstract: B4C–TiB2 composite ceramics, which are composed of TiB2 with high hardness and low density and B4C with ultrahigh hardness and ultralow density, represent typical structural composites featuring multifunctional characteristics, including high electrical conductivity, electrical discharge machinability, and excellent specific electromagnetic interference (EMI) shielding performance [1−5]. The integration of the structural and functional properties highlights the broad application prospects of B4C–TiB2 ceramics across diverse fields [6−8]. However, in practical engineering applications, ceramic materials often require fabrication into larger or more complex components. This makes the development of reliable joining techniques for B4C–TiB2 ceramics highly important.

abstract: Cellular ceramic structures (CCSs) fabricated by three-dimensional (3D) printing technologies are promising candidates for structural components, as they are lightweight and possess exceptional strength simultaneously [1]. Although notable achievements have been made in CCSs, achieving superior strength and damage resistance simultaneously remains a challenge for CCSs [2−4]. This is because the load-bearing capacity and damage tolerance of ceramics are mutually exclusive. Once overloaded, CCSs fail to dissipate excess energy and abruptly lose load-bearing capacity without warning. Such catastrophic failure severely restricts the application of CCSs. Therefore, enhancing the energy-absorbing ability of CCSs is the top priority to make them compelling candidates for structural components.

abstract: Accurate detection of formaldehyde (HCHO) is crucial, as HCHO is a common toxic gas released from interior decorations and incomplete combustion of fuel and tobacco leaves [1−4]. Long-term exposure to low concentrations of HCHO can cause chronic poisoning, damage to the body’s respiratory, nervous, and reproductive systems, and other diseases [5,6]. The World Health Organization (WHO) has established a recommended exposure limit for HCHO in indoor air of 0.08 ppm, as outlined in its Air Quality Guidelines, to safeguard public health; thus, HCHO has been identified as a hazardous substance by the WHO due to its carcinogenic and teratogenic effects [7,8]. Therefore, precise monitoring of low-concentration HCHO is highly important for human health [9,10].

abstract: ZrB2 is recognized as a promising material for ultrahigh-temperature structural components used in hypersonic vehicles, atmospheric re-entry, and rocket propulsion [1−4]. To satisfy the demands for load-bearing and reliability in these applications, ZrB2-based ceramics must have excellent mechanical properties, especially strength and toughness [5,6]. Owing to their high sensitivity to defects, ZrB2-based ceramics need to be prepared with low porosity to ensure these mechanical properties. However, high temperatures and long sintering time are usually required to densify ZrB2-based ceramics, which can cause significant grain coarsening and thus deteriorate their mechanical properties.

abstract: Temperature plays a pivotal role in the environment, directly affecting the survival, function, and overall health of organisms by shaping their physiological and behavioral responses. Likewise, pressure is an essential physical parameter, ranging from cosmic phenomena to complex biological processes within the human body. Both factors serve as critical indicators in health assessment, offering valuable data on functions such as breathing patterns, joint dynamics, and other vital activities [1]. As a result, the development of dual-mode sensors capable of detecting both temperature and pressure simultaneously has garnered significant attention. These advanced sensors hold immense potential in areas such as medical care, rehabilitation, human‒computer interaction, and flexible robotics.

abstract: Ultrahigh-temperature ceramics (UHTCs), which include transition metal carbides, diborides, and nitrides, are notable for their ultrahigh melting points and are widely applied in thermal protection systems within the aerospace and nuclear industries [1,2]. abstract: The introduction of zirconia-based ceramics, particularly yttria-stabilized tetragonal zirconia polycrystalline containing 3 mol% yttria (3Y-TZP), has revolutionized dentistry, enabling the development of all-ceramic crowns and fixed dental prostheses (FDPs) [1,2]. However, since TZP ceramics are generally opaque, an esthetic porcelain veneer layer is normally deposited on the surface to improve their aesthetic appearance. This veneer layer is susceptible to debonding or chipping because it is more prone to subcritical crack growth, leading to clinical restoration failure [1]. Therefore, a material that is highly strong and that maintains good translucency is required for dental applications.

abstract: Boride ceramics, renowned for their exceptional performance, span a spectrum from single-phase to composite and high-entropy formulations, serving as essential components in a diverse array of industries [1−10]. abstract: Thermal barrier coating (TBC) has the function of heat-resisting and heat-insulating at high temperatures because of its low thermal conductivity and high melting point [1]. TBC can be used not only for the thermal protection of the Ni-based superalloy above 1200 °C [1,2], but also for the thermal protection of light alloys, including magnesium alloy, aluminum alloy, and titanium alloy at relatively low temperatures [3−5]. A certain frequency range near the bottom of the millimeter-wave spectrum (30–80 GHz) is being used in the 5th generation cellular networks because of the enhanced spectrum bandwidth, which enables high-speed signal transmission [1−3]. To meet the needs of millimeter-wave applications, a low permittivity (*ε*r ≤ 15) for fast signal propagation speed, a high quality factor (*Q×f*) for better signal attenuation, and a near-zero temperature coefficient of the resonant frequency (*τ*f) for good operating environment stability of devices are the three most critical aspects [4,5].

abstract: Ferroelectric–phosphor composite materials have wide applications in optoelectronics and smart sensors [1−3] due to their excellent piezoelectric and luminescent properties. The approach frequently adopted to prepare ferroelectric–phosphor composite materials is to deposit a phosphor layer on the ferroelectric materials [4]. Zhang *et al*. [5] prepared a ZnS:Mn/PMN–PT composite material by depositing a ZnS:Mn phosphor thin film on a PMN–PT ferroelectric crystal via pulsed laser deposition. They observed dual-mode light and ultrasound emissions induced by the piezo–phototronic effect, which cannot be observed in single-phase phosphors or ferroelectric materials. However, the emission intensity is relatively weak due to the weak coupling between the ferroelectric and phosphor materials.

abstract: SiC-ceramic matrix composites (SiC-CMCs) are crucial materials for combustion components in gas turbine engines. These materials have melting points exceeding 2700 K and are extremely lightweight, providing excellent heat resistance and enhancing fuel efficiency [1−3]. However, SiC-CMC is susceptible to degradation in combustion environments containing high-temperature water vapor and oxygen [4,5]. Therefore, the surface should be covered with dense environmental barrier coatings (EBCs) to provide superior shielding against corrosive atmospheres for the application of hot section components [1,2,6].

abstract: Solid oxide fuel cells (SOFCs) are clean energy conversion devices capable of converting chemical energy stored in fuels directly into electrical energy without being limited by the Carnot cycle, resulting in high energy conversion efficiency [1−3]. Since the operating temperature of SOFCs is usually higher than 600 °C, they have a wide range of fuel flexibility [4,5]. Hydrogen (H2) is the simplest fuel for SOFCs, resulting in high performance and zero emission [6−8], but its production, transportation, and storage are not convenient for large-scale applications [9−11]. In contrast, hydrocarbon fuels, such as natural gas containing mainly methane (CH4), have abundant reserves, and their direct utilization is preferred for stationary power generation using SOFCs [12,13].
